sets.title: Finding the better deal
sets.summary: Students listen to a class use unit rates to choose between two notebook packs and answer questions about calculations, reasoning and a final argument, focusing on comparison language and explaining a mathematical choice.

script.title: Comparing Notebook Packs
script.setting: A math teacher and two students compare prices for a class supply drive.

lines.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
lines.text: Our class is collecting school supplies for the community center. We have 50 dollars to spend on notebooks. Today, we will use unit rates to decide which pack to buy.

lines.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
lines.text: Here are our 2 choices. Pack A has 4 notebooks for 6 dollars. Pack B has 10 notebooks for 12 dollars and 50 cents.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.text: At first, I thought Pack A was cheaper because 6 dollars is less than 12 dollars and 50 cents. But that compares the whole packs, not single notebooks.

lines.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
lines.text: Good thinking. So how do we compare them fairly?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: We find the unit price, which is the cost of 1 notebook. For Pack A, I divide 6 by 4. That equals 1 dollar and 50 cents per notebook. For Pack B, I divide 12 dollars and 50 cents by 10.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.text: So Pack B has the lower unit price. Each notebook in Pack B costs less.

lines.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
lines.text: Correct. Now think about our budget. With 50 dollars, we can buy exactly 4 packs of Pack B, which gives us 40 notebooks. With Pack A, we could buy 8 packs for 48 dollars.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.text: However, there is one more thing to think about. The community center said they need small notebooks for young children. Only Pack A has small notebooks.

lines.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
lines.text: That is an important point. The lowest unit price is not always the best choice. We also need to think about what the people we are helping actually need. Tomorrow, we will vote and explain our reasoning.

items.stem: What is the class buying for the community center?

choices.text: Pencils
choices.why: Pencils are school supplies, but the class is not buying pencils.
choices.misconception: Picks a related item that was not named

choices.text: Notebooks
choices.why: The teacher says the class has money to spend on notebooks.

choices.text: Paint
choices.why: Paint is never mentioned in the discussion.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

items.stem: How much money does the class have to spend?

choices.text: 50 dollars
choices.why: The teacher says the class has 50 dollars to spend.

choices.text: 6 dollars
choices.why: 6 dollars is the price of one pack, not the class budget.
choices.misconception: Picks a number that was said for a different quantity

choices.text: 48 dollars
choices.why: 48 dollars is the cost of one possible purchase, not the total budget.
choices.misconception: Confuses an amount spent with the amount available

items.stem: Why does Hana say her first idea was not a fair comparison?

choices.text: Pack A has fewer notebooks, so it must cost more per notebook.
choices.why: Having fewer items does not decide the unit price, and Hana does not say this.
choices.misconception: Reasons from an unrelated feature of the data

choices.text: She used the wrong prices from the table.
choices.why: Hana used the correct prices; the problem was what she compared.
choices.misconception: Adds an error that was not described

choices.text: It compared the prices of whole packs, not the price of 1 notebook.
choices.why: Hana explains that she compared the whole packs instead of single notebooks.

choices.text: The two packs cost the same amount.
choices.why: The packs have different prices.
choices.misconception: Misremembers the numbers that were said

items.stem: Mateo divides 12 dollars and 50 cents by 10. What is the unit price of Pack B?

choices.text: $1.50 per notebook
choices.why: This is the unit price Mateo found for the other pack.
choices.misconception: Matches a result to the wrong option

choices.text: $12.50 per notebook
choices.why: This is the price of the whole pack, not of 1 notebook.
choices.misconception: Uses the total instead of the unit rate

choices.text: $1.20 per notebook
choices.why: This divides only 12 by 10 and leaves out the 50 cents.
choices.misconception: Drops the cents and divides only the whole dollars

choices.text: $1.25 per notebook
choices.why: 12.50 divided by 10 notebooks is 1.25 dollars for each notebook.

items.stem: Mr. Alvarez says the class could buy 8 packs of Pack A. How many notebooks would that be?

choices.text: 32 notebooks
choices.why: Each Pack A has 4 notebooks, and 8 packs of 4 is 32 notebooks.

choices.text: 40 notebooks
choices.why: 40 is the number of notebooks from the other pack.
choices.misconception: Matches a result to the wrong option

choices.text: 8 notebooks
choices.why: 8 is the number of packs, not the number of notebooks.
choices.misconception: Confuses the number of groups with the total

choices.text: 33 notebooks
choices.why: Dividing 50 by the unit price ignores that notebooks come in whole packs of 4.
choices.misconception: Ignores that items are sold in whole packs

items.stem: What is Mr. Alvarez's main point at the end of the discussion?

choices.text: The class should always buy the pack with the lowest unit price.
choices.why: The teacher says the lowest unit price is not always the best choice.
choices.misconception: Over-generalizes into a rule the speaker rejects

choices.text: Pack A is the better deal because it costs less per notebook.
choices.why: The class found that Pack A costs more per notebook.
choices.misconception: Reverses the result of the comparison

choices.text: A good decision uses math and also considers what people need.
choices.why: The teacher says they need to think about unit price and what the people they help actually need.

choices.text: The class does not have enough money for either pack.
choices.why: The class can afford several packs of either kind.
choices.misconception: Contradicts the numbers in the discussion

sets.title: How a river town grew
sets.summary: Students listen to a class read three historical maps of a fictional town and answer questions about chronology, population change and cause and effect, focusing on time words and causal language for narrating history.

script.title: Three Maps of Millbrook
script.setting: A social studies teacher and two students compare three maps of a fictional town.

lines.speaker: Ms. Petrova
lines.text: Today we will trace the history of a fictional town called Millbrook using 3 maps. Each map shows the town at a different time. Listen for how the town changed and why.

lines.speaker: Ms. Petrova
lines.text: The first map is from 1850. Millbrook was a small farming village on the east bank of the Silver River. About 300 people lived there. Families settled near the river because they needed water for crops and animals.

lines.speaker: Aiyana
lines.text: On the second map, from 1900, I notice a railroad line and a large mill next to the river. The population grew to 4,000 people.

lines.speaker: Ms. Petrova
lines.text: That is correct. The railroad arrived in 1885. After that, farmers could ship their crops to cities quickly. The mill also created jobs, so many new workers moved to Millbrook.

lines.speaker: Kwame
lines.text: The third map is from today. The mill is gone, and there is a park along the river instead. Also, the town spread to the west bank, and there is a highway.

lines.speaker: Ms. Petrova
lines.text: Good observation. The mill closed in 1970, and many people lost their jobs. For a while, the population went down. However, in the 1990s, the town turned the old mill land into a riverside park and a community college.

lines.speaker: Aiyana
lines.text: So the river was important in every time period, but people used it in different ways. First, it was for farming. Then, it powered the mill. Now, it is a place for people to relax.

lines.speaker: Ms. Petrova
lines.text: Exactly. Your task is to write a short history of Millbrook. Use time words, such as first, later and finally, and explain the causes of each change.

items.stem: What does the class use to learn about Millbrook?

choices.text: A globe
choices.why: A globe shows the whole world, and the class does not use one.
choices.misconception: Picks a related tool that was not named

choices.text: Books
choices.why: The discussion does not mention books.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

choices.text: Maps
choices.why: The teacher says the class will use 3 maps.

choices.text: A busy town with a large mill
choices.why: The mill appears on a later map.
choices.misconception: Confuses the time periods

choices.text: A small farming village
choices.why: The teacher says Millbrook was a small farming village in 1850.

choices.text: A town with a highway and a park
choices.why: These are features of the map from today.
choices.misconception: Confuses the time periods

items.stem: According to Ms. Petrova, what happened after the railroad arrived in 1885?

choices.text: Farmers could ship their crops to cities quickly.
choices.why: The teacher says that after the railroad arrived, farmers could ship crops to cities quickly.

choices.text: The mill closed and many people lost their jobs.
choices.why: This happened much later, in 1970.
choices.misconception: Confuses the sequence of events

choices.text: Families moved to the west bank to start farms.
choices.why: The town spread to the west bank later, and the talk does not link it to farming.
choices.misconception: Combines details from different time periods

choices.text: The river stopped being important to the town.
choices.why: The discussion says the river stayed important.
choices.misconception: Contradicts what was said

items.stem: How did the population of Millbrook change between 1850 and 1900?

choices.text: It went down because the mill closed.
choices.why: The population went down in a different time period.
choices.misconception: Applies an event to the wrong time period

choices.text: It grew from about 300 to 1,900 people.
choices.why: 1900 is a year on the map, not the number of people.
choices.misconception: Confuses a year with a population number

choices.text: It stayed about the same.
choices.why: The numbers given for the two maps are very different.
choices.misconception: Misses the change in the data

choices.text: It grew from about 300 to 4,000 people.
choices.why: The town had about 300 people in 1850 and 4,000 people in 1900.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes a cause-and-effect relationship in Millbrook's history?

choices.text: Because the population went down, the railroad arrived.
choices.why: The railroad came during a time of growth, and it was not caused by a smaller population.
choices.misconception: Links events that were not connected

choices.text: Because the mill closed, many people lost their jobs.
choices.why: The teacher says the mill closed, people lost jobs, and the population went down for a while.

choices.text: Because the park was built, the mill closed.
choices.why: The park was built on the land after the mill had already closed.
choices.misconception: Reverses cause and effect

choices.text: Because of the highway, families first settled near the river.
choices.why: Families settled near the river long before the highway, and for a different reason.
choices.misconception: Ignores the order of events

items.stem: What is Aiyana's main idea about the river?

choices.text: The river was only important while the mill was open.
choices.why: Aiyana says the river was important in every time period.
choices.misconception: Narrows the idea to one time period

choices.text: People stopped using the river after 1970.
choices.why: Today people use the riverside park, so they still use the river.
choices.misconception: Over-generalizes from one event

choices.text: The river moved from the east bank to the west bank.
choices.why: The town spread to the west bank; the river did not move.
choices.misconception: Misunderstands what changed on the map

choices.text: Its uses changed, but it stayed important to the town.
choices.why: Aiyana says the river was used for farming, then the mill, and now for relaxing.

sets.title: Which cup keeps heat in?
sets.summary: Students listen to two classmates debate whether their heat investigation supports a claim and answer questions about data, fair tests and evaluating evidence, focusing on argument language such as claim, evidence, however and if.

script.title: Is Our Claim Strong?
script.setting: A science teacher talks with two students about the results of a heat investigation.

lines.speaker: Mr. Osei
lines.text: Yesterday, your group tested which cup keeps hot water warm the longest. You poured water at 80 degrees Celsius into 3 cups. After 20 minutes, you measured the temperature again. Rafael, what is your group's claim?

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.text: Our claim is that the foam cup is the best insulator. The water in the foam cup dropped to 68 degrees. The paper cup dropped to 55 degrees, and the metal cup dropped to 49 degrees. The foam cup lost the least heat, so it is the best.

lines.speaker: Lina
lines.text: I agree that the foam cup kept the water warmest. However, I am not sure our test was fair. The foam cup had a plastic lid, but the other 2 cups did not have lids.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.text: Why does that matter? The lid is just a small piece of plastic.

lines.speaker: Lina
lines.text: A lid stops warm air from escaping at the top. So we cannot tell if the foam or the lid kept the heat in. We changed 2 variables at the same time.

lines.speaker: Mr. Osei
lines.text: That is a strong piece of reasoning, Lina. In a fair test, you change only 1 variable and keep everything else the same. What else could make your evidence stronger?

lines.speaker: Lina
lines.text: We only did each test 1 time. If we repeat the test 3 times and get similar results, we can trust them more.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.text: Okay, I see the problem. Next time, we will test all 3 cups with no lids, and we will repeat it 3 times. If the foam cup still loses the least heat, our claim will be much stronger.

lines.speaker: Mr. Osei
lines.text: Excellent. Remember, a claim is only as strong as the evidence and reasoning behind it.

choices.text: Temperature
choices.why: The teacher says the group measured the temperature of the water.

choices.text: Length
choices.why: The group did not measure how long anything was.
choices.misconception: Picks a different kind of measurement

choices.text: Weight
choices.why: The discussion never mentions weighing the cups.
choices.misconception: Adds information that was not said

items.stem: Which cup kept the water the warmest?

choices.text: The paper cup
choices.why: The paper cup was in the middle, not the warmest.
choices.misconception: Picks the middle value

choices.text: The metal cup
choices.why: The metal cup had the lowest temperature at the end.
choices.misconception: Confuses warmest with coolest

choices.text: The foam cup
choices.why: The water in the foam cup stayed at the highest temperature.

items.stem: The water started at 80 degrees. How many degrees did the water in the foam cup cool in 20 minutes?

choices.text: 68 degrees
choices.why: 68 degrees is the final temperature, not how much it cooled.
choices.misconception: Gives the final value instead of the change

choices.text: 12 degrees
choices.why: The water went from 80 to 68 degrees, and 80 minus 68 is 12.

choices.text: 25 degrees
choices.why: This is the change for a different cup.
choices.misconception: Uses data for the wrong cup

choices.text: 20 degrees
choices.why: 20 is the number of minutes, not degrees.
choices.misconception: Confuses time with temperature

items.stem: Why does Lina think the test was not fair?

choices.text: The foam cup started with hotter water.
choices.why: All 3 cups started with water at the same temperature.
choices.misconception: Contradicts a detail that was said

choices.text: The lid was just a small piece of plastic.
choices.why: Rafael says this to argue that the lid does not matter.
choices.misconception: Picks a detail that was said but does not answer

choices.text: They measured the cups at different times.
choices.why: All the cups were measured after 20 minutes.
choices.misconception: Invents a measuring error

choices.text: Only the foam cup had a lid on top of it.
choices.why: Lina says the group changed 2 variables, the cup and the lid, at the same time.

items.stem: Which plan would best test Rafael's claim?

choices.text: Put lids on only the paper cup and the metal cup.
choices.why: The cups would still be different in 2 ways, so the test would not be fair.
choices.misconception: Keeps 2 variables changing at once

choices.text: Test the foam cup again with a bigger lid.
choices.why: Testing only one cup cannot show which cup is best.
choices.misconception: Tests one condition without a comparison

choices.text: Test all 3 cups with no lids, 3 times each.
choices.why: This changes only the cup material and repeats the test, as Lina and Rafael describe.

choices.text: Use hotter water in the metal cup to make it fair.
choices.why: Changing the starting temperature adds a new variable.
choices.misconception: Misunderstands what makes a test fair

items.stem: How does Rafael's thinking change during the discussion?

choices.text: He decides that the paper cup is the best insulator.
choices.why: Rafael never says the paper cup is best.
choices.misconception: Adds a conclusion that was not said

choices.text: He moves from being sure of his claim to planning a fairer test.
choices.why: Rafael starts by defending his claim and ends by planning a test with no lids and 3 trials.

choices.text: He starts by saying the lid matters and ends by saying it does not.
choices.why: This is backward; he first said the lid did not matter.
choices.misconception: Reverses the order of ideas

choices.text: He stays sure that his first test was fair.
choices.why: Rafael says he sees the problem, so his thinking does change.
choices.misconception: Misses the change in the speaker's view
